title: A Warm and Koji Thanksgiving: Add a Hint of Japanese Curry to Your Gravy
contentHtml:
Turkey or chicken gravy get a quick boost of flavor from a Japanese curry roux block and a small splash of cider vinegar.

A few weeks back, Lena—my head of operations, a chef extraordinaire, and JKLA World HQ's resident Canadian—had just returned from a trip to the True North where she had partaken in the hugely less commercial and equally historically problematic version of Thanksgiving celebrated up there. She came back with lots of turkey to recipe test with (my normal turkey supplier couldn’t get the goods in time for testing this year) and a new recipe idea inspired by one she had made for her own family: Japanese curry gravy.

Not Japanese curry sauce, per se, but a rich, dark, roasty turkey gravy with just a hint of Japanese curry flavor peeking through.

The concept sounded delicious to me and given that my new Koji-Brined Roast Turkey this year is already leaning heavily into Japanese flavors and ingredients, a curry-spiked gravy seemed like the perfect match.

I did a bit of experimenting with the gravy in the kitchen. In the most basic version, I started with my Easy Turkey Gravy, swapping out a tablespoon of flour in the roux for a single Japanese curry block dissolved into four cups of gravy, resulting in a sauce that clearly tasted like Japanese curry, but was subtle enough that it still worked with all of my other standard Thanksgiving sides. At Lena’s suggestion, I added just the faintest touch of apple cider vinegar which immediately livened the whole thing up.

In one version I pulsed mirepoix vegetables—carrots, onions, and celery—down in a food processor then let the mixture sweat out in butter before adding flour, dark turkey stock, and a cube of Japanese curry roux. I loved the texture and flavor the little bits of vegetables lent to the gravy, even if it wasn’t traditionally smooth in texture.

In a third version, I used some of the massive stockpile of dark roux I have after recipe testing for an upcoming gumbo recipe (psst… the best way to make a dark roux is by toasting the dry flour in the oven). This may have been my favorite yet, with a nice nutty, toasty flavor from the dark roux that pairs nicely with the warm spices of the curry.

The point is, if you're a Japanese curry lover, there’s not really a wrong way to do this. Take your favorite gravy, add a bit o’ curry and a touch of acid, and you’re in business.

I did find myself craving a bit of fukujinzuke—the pickles traditionally served with Japanese curry—which got me thinking: How would this work with a shiso-flavored cranberry pickle?

Sounds like a project for next year.

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • A single square of Japanese curry roux adds warm spice and savory depth to your favorite gravy without overwhelming the roasty turkey flavor. 

  • A little cider vinegar brightens it all up.

Yield: About 4 cups
Active Time: 5 minutes
Total Time: 10 minutes
Notes: Use your favorite homemade or store-bought turkey or chicken gravy. Japanese curry roux comes in segmented blocks. Use one block per four cups of gravy. The roux will thicken your gravy slightly; thin it with stock or water as needed. If making gravy from scratch specifically for this recipe, you can reduce the flour in your usual recipe by 1 tablespoon.

Ingredients

  • 4 cups (or 1 liter) turkey or chicken gravy

  • 1 square Japanese curry roux, such as S&B Golden Curry or Vermont Curry, roughly chopped

  • 1 teaspoon (5ml) apple cider vinegar, plus more to taste

  • Turkey or chicken stock or water, as needed

  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper

Method

  1. Add the curry. Bring the gravy to a simmer in a medium saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally. Add the curry roux and whisk until completely dissolved. Simmer, stirring frequently, until smooth, about 5 minutes.

  2. Adjust and serve. Stir in the cider vinegar. Thin with stock or water as needed until the gravy reaches your preferred consistency, then season to taste with salt and pepper. Serve hot.
